hero.kicker: Mulching in St. Clair Shores, MI and across Metro Detroit
hero.title: Fresh mulch. **No volcanoes.**
hero.lede: HD Landscape keeps it simple: two to three inches of fresh mulch, spread clean and kept off the trunks and stems, with the weeds out and the bed line cut first. Mulch spreading is the job our Google reviews bring up most.

blocks.title: Most mulch problems are **too much mulch.**
body: HD Landscape spreads fresh mulch in St. Clair Shores and across Metro Detroit, at the two to three inches Michigan State University Extension recommends. At that depth mulch holds moisture in the ground and slows weeds. In one MSU trial, properly mulched plots outgrew plots with no mulch, even when the bare plots were kept weed free.

The usual mistake is adding a full layer every spring. MSU Extension is plain about it: two to three inches is adequate, and more is not better. Heaped on year after year, mulch can smother perennials and cake into a layer that sheds rain. The other classic is the mulch volcano, mounded up against a tree trunk, where the dark, damp bark invites rot and insects. So look at what is already in a bed before anything new goes on it.

blocks.title: Four steps. **The mulch is third.**

steps.title: Check
steps.body: How much mulch is already there decides the job. A bed with good depth needs only a light top up. One that is deep or crusted should be broken up and pulled back first, so water can reach the soil again.

steps.title: Pull and edge
steps.body: [Weeds come out](/weeding/) by hand, roots included, because established weeds push through fresh mulch. Then the bed line gets cut clean. If you want a permanent line, ask about [steel edging](/steel-edging/).

steps.title: Spread
steps.body: Mulch goes down even, two to three inches in the open bed. Near a tree it tapers down and stays off the bark. MSU Extension's number is a six inch mulch free ring around the trunk. Shrubs and perennials get room at the stems too.

steps.title: Clean up
steps.body: Walks, drives and lawn get cleaned off before the crew leaves. One customer's review put it simply: "how clean they left the job."

blocks.footnote: Depth and trunk spacing come from Michigan State University Extension guidance. If a tree in your yard already has mulch piled against it, ask and we will pull it back.

blocks.title: Done right, you notice **the plants first.**
blocks.intro: Black on some homes, brown on others. Either one makes green plants and a clean edge stand out.

blocks.title: Not every bed gets the same mulch job.

items.title: Landscape fabric under mulch
items.body: It is not the fix it looks like. Penn State Extension says woven fabric keeps water, worms and soil microbes from moving freely through the soil. Over time roots knit into it from above and below, and it gets very hard to remove. Ask Jake before you buy a roll.

items.title: Mulch or stone
items.body: Mulch breaks down and feeds the soil, so it needs freshening. Stone does not break down, but it adds nothing to the soil either. Planted beds usually do better in mulch. For a low care strip along a walk or a drive, look at [rock and stone](/rock-and-stone-installation/).

items.title: Beds that stay wet
items.body: Clay is common around here, and it drains slowly. Penn State Extension says to use less mulch on poorly drained soil, so a soggy bed gets a lighter layer. If water sits there, [grading](/yard-grading/) may be the real fix.

items.title: Ground nesting bees
items.body: MSU Extension suggests watching your beds on warm, sunny spring days before you mulch. Where bees are nesting, a thinner layer of one to two inches is better. Tell us where they are and we will go light.

blocks.title: In St. Clair Shores, check the depth first.
body: HD Landscape is based in St. Clair Shores, and it is one of the towns we work in most. The city grew quickly from a resort community after World War II, so a lot of homes here have beds that have been around for decades. A bed topped off every spring for that long can build up well past the point of helping, which is why depth is the first thing to look at.

The ground here points the same way. USDA soil data shows heavy, poorly drained ground across most of the city, on very little slope, so a bed that stays wet should get less mulch, not more. If your yard runs down to the lake or a canal, keep mulch away from the water, which is the advice in the waterfront guide the city posts.

Inland lots can run as small as 6,000 square feet, so beds sit close to walks, drives and the neighbors, and the mulch has to stay in the bed. We also mulch beds in [Grosse Pointe](/service-areas/grosse-pointe/), [Birmingham](/service-areas/birmingham/) and towns across Macomb and Oakland counties.

blocks.title: On time, with good advice first.

faq.q: Do you do mulching in St. Clair Shores?
faq.a: Yes. HD Landscape is based in St. Clair Shores and spreads mulch for homes here and across the Grosse Pointes, Macomb County and Oakland County. Mulching is one of the jobs our customers mention most.

Two to three inches in most beds. Michigan State University Extension says that is adequate and that more is not better. If a bed already has mulch in it, about an inch is enough to freshen it without piling up depth.

faq.q: How far should mulch stay from a tree trunk?
faq.a: MSU Extension says about six inches: keep a mulch free ring around the trunk and let the layer taper down as it gets close. Its shorthand is a doughnut, not a volcano. Shrub stems need room at the base as well.

faq.q: What is a mulch volcano, and why is it bad?
faq.a: A mulch volcano is mulch mounded up against a tree trunk. It keeps the bark dark and damp, which invites rot and insects, and it encourages roots to grow up into the mulch where they do not belong. If you have one, we can pull it back.

faq.q: Do you remove the old mulch first?
faq.a: Usually it does not all need to go. Old mulch breaks down into the soil, which is part of why it is good for a bed. If a bed has built up too deep or crusted over, it should be broken up and the extra pulled back before anything new goes on.

faq.q: When should I mulch in Michigan?
faq.a: Mid spring is the usual time, once the soil has warmed up, and it pairs well with a [spring cleanup](/spring-and-fall-cleanups/). Beds can be freshened in fall too. A layer of mulch also insulates the soil, which helps protect roots from an early freeze.

It helps a lot, within limits. Two to three inches can smother annual weeds and some perennials, and a light top up each year keeps new seeds from sprouting. Established perennial weeds push through, so they have to come out first. That is why a bed should be [weeded](/weeding/) before it gets mulch.

faq.q: How much mulch do I need for my beds?
faq.a: One cubic yard covers about 160 square feet at two inches, or about 108 square feet at three inches. You do not have to work it out, though. The amount goes on your estimate.

faq.q: What kind of mulch should I use?
faq.a: MSU Extension says the type of organic mulch matters less than the fact that plants are mulched. Color is mostly taste, and Jake can help you pick what suits the house. The one thing to watch is quality, because MSU warns that poor mulch can bring in weeds such as mugwort and Canada thistle.

faq.q: Will mulch attract termites to my house?
faq.a: University of Florida guidance says the bigger risk is termites already on your property, more than stragglers in the mulch. It recommends less than two inches of mulch within a foot of the foundation and at least six inches of clear space below the siding, so any activity can be seen. Ask and we will keep the layer light along the house.

faq.q: How long does a mulch job take?
faq.a: A normal set of beds can often be done in a day. A big property, or beds that need heavy weeding first, can take longer, which is one more reason Jake walks the beds before he writes anything down.

Three things set the price: how much bed there is, how much mulch is already down and how much weeding comes first. Jake looks at all three in person, and his free estimate is itemized so you can go through it line by line.
